section: pre1 (pre-chorus 1), 44.65-59.42 s, bars 24-31, lyric lines 24-31 (0-based), scene file src/scenes/04_pre1.js
summary: Four shots of 8 beats each (3.69 s), all hard cuts that land exactly on a cursor click: the user opens a 616 px settings drawer on the AI and works down its five rows (Current AC/DC, Vision, Knowledge date, Shared memory, Context depth). The cursor is the protagonist; the AI only narrates in orange serif, either on the page top-left (wide shots) or as a 24 px annotation under the row being touched (close shots). The section uses NO character art at all (room() is called without art; env.art is not even destructured), so the anime-illustration complaint does not apply here and nothing has to be swapped. There are no ALL-CAPS keyword lines in lines 24-31; the "hits" are the clicks. Shots 1, 2 and 4 are strong and varied (wide drawer + live graph / 2.96x macro with full-frame mosaic and camera kicks / centred sheet with the spark-and-dot pair and a fly-through). Shot 3 (pre1-date) is the calmest and most diagram-like of the four: a grey 560 px band with two static 204 px serif era tokens, a thin ruler and a year counter; only a 46 px spark slides along it.

diagnosis:
(a) The "Current" click. Frames at 49.68-51.55 show the cursor leaving the Vision row twice. At 49.96-50.10 it hovers on the DC half of the Current control in a perfectly clear frame (waypoint b(11.5), no click), and at 50.65 (beat 13) it clicks the AC half. That click happens while Vision is off, so the frame is 56 px mosaic: the cream click burst, the brightest thing in the picture, lands on an unreadable orange block in the top third, roughly 120 world px (about 360 screen px at 2.96x) above the toggle and far from the wobbling lyric. A viewer cannot tell what was clicked; the mosaic does not change on that beat (only Vision clicks switch it), so beat 13 reads as a miss in an otherwise clear on/off pattern; and when sight returns at 51.25 the Current control has silently changed from DC to AC. The lyric being sung is the dizzy line, which is drawn under the Vision row and whose whole effect (blind/see, camera kicks) is driven by the Vision toggle. So the idea "one switch is rattled until it is dizzy" is diluted by a zig-zag to another row. The director's wish is exactly what the frames suggest: every hit of this phrase on the Vision toggle.
(b) The date shot. What the frames show is a settings diagram, not a journey. The band takes only about half the frame height; the top and bottom quarters are a dimmed leftover of the client (46 % of the frame carries nothing). Inside the band both era tokens are on screen from the first frame, so the destination is known before the trip starts and crossing the line is only a brightness swap. The only moving things are a 46 px spark on a 6 px line and a number in the corner; the camera moves 3.5 %. Of the 3.69 s, real travel is about 0.9 s (53.42-54.34); the knob is almost still for 0.46 s (52.96-53.42) and parked for 0.58 s (54.34-54.92), then 0.8 s goes to folding the band and a plain wide frame. At contact-sheet size six of the eight beat frames look the same. There is no picture of time or history (no era imagery, no clock, no speed, no depth), and the single accent (53.81) sits 0.07 s before beat 20. Its neighbours are much louder: pre1-vision changes the whole frame on every click, pre1-unite has a glowing centre motif and a fly-through. So the lyric with the most cinematic potential in the section gets the flattest picture, which is the director's "not strong enough".
What is strong: the concept and its logic (the knob IS the spark, the user's hand drags the AI into the past; ticks right of the knob go dim because that time is no longer known), the cut on the grab with the knob match-cut, the band opening out of and folding back into its own drawer row, the era tokens being the lyric's own words, the mono year counter, strict colour roles, and the whole of shots 1, 2 (minus the Current detour) and 4.
